flora.name: Dandelion
flora.identification: Yellow flower head, lobed leaves form a rosette at base, hollow milky stem.
flora.uses: Leaves in salad, roots roasted for 'coffee', flowers for jelly.
flora.caution: Ensure area hasn't been sprayed with pesticides.

details.harvesting: Harvest leaves in early spring (pre-flower) for less bitterness. Dig roots in late fall for highest medicinal potency/starch.
processing: **Coffee Substitute:** Scrub roots, chop into small pieces, roast at 400°F until dark brown and brittle. Grind and brew like coffee.
**Greens:** Blanch for 2 mins to remove bitterness, then sauté with garlic or add to stews.
**Salve:** Infuse wilted flowers in oil for 2 weeks. Strain. Melt beeswax (1 part wax to 4 parts oil) into it. Good for sore muscles and dry skin.
**Fritters:** Dip fresh flower heads in batter and fry. Tastes like mushrooms.

flora.name: Stinging Nettle
flora.identification: Serrated leaves, tiny stinging hairs on stems and leaves. Square stem.
flora.uses: Cooked like spinach (destroys sting), high iron tea, cordage from stems.
flora.caution: Must be cooked/dried. Wear gloves. 'Dock leaf' often grows nearby to soothe stings.

details.habitat: Nitrogen-rich soil, near old homesteads, compost piles, riverbanks.
details.harvesting: Wear gloves! Harvest top 4-6 leaves in spring before flowering. For cordage, harvest tall stalks in autumn.
processing: **Eating:** Steam or boil for 2 minutes to destroy stinging hairs (formic acid). Use essentially like spinach. Very high in Iron and Vitamin C.
**Tea:** Dry leaves for winter tea. Good for allergies (antihistamine).
**Cordage (Rope):** Harvest tall mature stalks. Strip leaves. Crush stem to split it. Peel outer fibers from the woody core. Twist fibers together (reverse wrap) to make strong string.

flora.name: Cattail
flora.identification: Tall reed in water, brown 'cigar' seed head.
flora.uses: Spring shoots (raw), Pollen (flour), Roots (starch), Fluff (insulation).
flora.caution: Ensure water source is not polluted (bio-accumulator). Lookalikes: Iris (toxic).

processing: **Early Spring (Shoots):** Peel outer leaves of young shoots to find the tender white 'Cossack Asparagus' core. Eat raw or cooked.
**Summer (Pollen):** Shake yellow pollen from top flower spike into a bag. Mix 50/50 with flour for pancakes/bread.
**Fall/Winter (Roots/Rhizomes):** Dig up mud. Wash roots. Mash in water to settle out the starch. Dry the white starch to make flour.
**Winter (Fluff):** The brown cigar explodes into fluff. Excellent tinder or insulation for jackets/bedding (warning: extremely flammable).

flora.name: White Willow
flora.identification: Tree near water, lance-shaped leaves with white underside.
flora.uses: Bark contains Salicin (Aspirin). Chew twig for pain/fever relief.
flora.caution: Blood thinner. Do not use if allergic to aspirin.

processing: **Pain Relief:** Peel small strips of inner bark from young twigs. Chew directly for toothache/headache.
**Tea:** Simmer (decoction) bark for 10-15 minutes. Bitter but effective for fevers.
**Rooting Hormone:** Soak chopped willow tips in water for 24 hours. Water cuttings with this 'willow water' to help them root.

flora.name: Broadleaf Plantain
flora.identification: Low rosette, oval leaves with distinct parallel ribs.
flora.uses: 'Green Band-Aid'. Chew leaf into poultice for bee stings, bites, and cuts.
flora.caution: Wash thoroughly. Ensure the collection area is free from animal waste, pesticides, and road runoff.

processing: **Poultice (Spit Poultice):** Chew a clean leaf until it's a green mush. Place directly on bee sting, splinter, or infected cut. Bandage in place. Draws out toxins and infection.
**Seeds:** When seed stalks turn brown, strip seeds. High in fiber (psyllium husk precursor).

flora.name: Yarrow
flora.identification: Feathery fern-like leaves, flat cluster of white flowers.
flora.uses: Styptic (stops bleeding). Pack into deep wounds. Fever reducer tea.
flora.caution: Lookalikes: Hemlock (deadly). Yarrow has feathery leaves, Hemlock has carrot-like leaves. Smell test: Yarrow smells herbal/aromatic.

processing: **Stop Bleeding:** Crush fresh leaves and flowers. Pack tightly into a deep wound to clot blood instantly.
**Fever Tea:** Steep flowers/leaves in hot water. Induces sweating to break a fever.
**Repellent:** Rub crushed plant on skin/clothes to repel mosquitoes.

flora.name: Mullein
flora.identification: Tall stalk (year 2), fuzzy soft 'lamb's ear' leaves.
flora.uses: Leaves for respiratory tea (filter hairs). Flower stalk dip in fat for torch. 'Cowboy Toilet Paper'.
flora.caution: Tiny hairs can irritate throat - ensure tea is filtered well.

processing: **Tea:** Good for coughs/lungs. Must strain through coffee filter/cloth to remove irritating hairs.
**Ear Oil:** Infuse yellow flowers in olive oil / bear grease. Use drops for ear infections.
**Torch:** Dip the dried 2nd-year stalk in melted pine resin or animal fat. Burns for a long time.

flora.name: White Pine
flora.identification: Needles in bundles of 5. Long cones.
flora.uses: Needle tea (Vitamin C). Resin for glue/fire starter. Inner bark (famine food).
flora.caution: Lookalike: Yew (flat needles, red berries) is DEADLY.

processing: **Tea:** Steep (don't boil) green needles in hot water. 5x more Vitamin C than lemons. Good for scurvy prevention.
**Resin Glue (Pitch Sticks):** Melt hardened resin + charcoal dust + rabbit scat/dried grass (binder). roll onto a stick. Heating it makes it sticky glue.
**Fire:** Resin is highly flammable even when wet.

flora.name: Jewelweed
flora.identification: Tall, translucent stem, orange trumpet flowers. Grows near Poison Ivy.
flora.uses: The Antidote. Crush stem juice onto Poison Ivy rash immediately.
flora.caution: For topical use only; do not ingest. Ensure correct identification to avoid other orange-flowered plants.

details.habitat: Shady, wet areas. Often right next to Poison Ivy.
processing: **Poison Ivy Cure:** Crush the hollow stems to release the orange/clear juice. Rub vigorously on skin that touched Poison Ivy. It creates a soapy lather that binds to the oil and washes it off.
**Ice Cubes:** Blend entire plant with water, strain, and freeze into cubes. Rub on rashes/bug bites later in the year.

flora.name: Poison Hemlock
flora.identification: Purple splotches on smooth hairless stem. Fern-like leaves. White umbrella flowers. Musty smell.
flora.uses: NONE - DEADLY neurotoxin.
flora.caution: Do not touch. Can be fatal if eaten (mistaken for wild carrot).

details.processing: STAY AWAY. Even dead stalks can remain toxic for years. If you touch it, wash hands immediately. Do not burn (smoke is toxic).

flora.name: Poison Ivy
flora.identification: Leaves of three, shiny. vine or shrub. 'Hairy' vine on trees.
flora.uses: NONE.
flora.caution: Oil (Urushiol) causes blistering rash. Wash with cold water and soap within 15 mins.

details.habitat: Edge spaces, climbing trees, ground cover.
details.processing: If exposed: Wash with COLD water (hot opens pores) and lots of soap (dish soap is best) within 15 minutes. Scrub with a washcloth to physically remove the oil.

flora.name: Chicory
flora.identification: Bright blue daisy-like flowers on stiff stalks. jagged leaves like dandelion.
flora.uses: Root roasted for coffee substitute. Young leaves for salad.
flora.caution: Excessive consumption may cause mild digestive upset. Consult a healthcare professional if pregnant or nursing.

processing: **Coffee:** Dig taproot. Scrub clean. Chop. Roast until brittle/dark. Grind. Brews a dark, rich, caffeine-free coffee.
**Greens:** Harvest young leaves in spring. Bitter but nutritious. Boil to mellow flavor.

flora.name: Wild Garlic / Onion
flora.identification: Hollow, round leaves (chives). Smells strongly of onion/garlic when crushed.
flora.uses: Flavoring, immune booster, antibiotic.
flora.caution: Lookalike: Death Camas (looks similar but has NO garlic smell). If it doesn't smell like garlic, DO NOT EAT IT.

processing: **Bulbs:** Dig up clumps. Wash. Use like green onions.
**Medicine:** Raw garlic is purely antibiotic/antiviral. Eat a clove daily if sick.

flora.name: Burdock
flora.identification: Huge rhubarb-like leaves. Purple thistle flowers (burrs that stick to clothes).
flora.uses: Root is a substantial calorie source. Blood purifier.
flora.caution: Diuretic effect. Digging deep taproots requires caution to avoid muscle strain or contact with soil pathogens.

processing: **Root:** Dig deep taproot (can be 2ft long) in 1st year (no flower stalk). Peel thick skin. Boil or roast. Tastes earthy/nutty (Gobo root).
**Leaves:** Poultice for burns/rashes.

flora.name: Elderberry
flora.identification: Shrub with clusters of tiny dark purple berries. Flat white flower clusters.
flora.uses: Flu/Cold remedy (Syrup). Immune support.
flora.caution: CRITICAL: MUST BE COOKED. Raw berries, seeds, leaves, and bark contain cyanogenic glycosides (cyanide-inducing). Ingestion can cause severe nausea and vomiting. Identify carefully: Elderberry stems have white pith; LOOKALIKE Water Hemlock has hollow stems and is DEADLY.

processing: **Syrup:** Simmer ripe berries with water for at least 45 mins. This heat destroys the toxins. Mash and strain. Add honey (preservative). Take 1 tsp daily for immune support.
**Safety Rule:** Never consume green berries. Only harvest deep purple/black clusters.

**Lookalike Check:** Ensure you are NOT looking at Water Hemlock. Elderberry is a woody shrub with opposite leaves and white pith; Water Hemlock is an herbaceous plant with a hollow, often purple-spotted stem and is one of the most poisonous plants in North America.

flora.name: Lamb's Quarters
flora.identification: Diamond shaped leaves with white mealy/dusty coating underneath.
flora.uses: Wild Spinach. Seeds are like Quinoa.
flora.caution: Absorbs nitrates from soil (don't harvest near fertilized farm fields).

processing: **Greens:** Steam leaves. Richer in Calcium/Protein than spinach.
**Seeds:** Harvest in fall. Rub chaff off. Boil like quinoa/porridge.

flora.name: Amadou (Horse Hoof Fungus)
flora.identification: Grey, hoof-shaped fungus growing on dead/dying Birch or Beech trees.
flora.uses: Fire starter (takes a spark instantly). Hat making (felt).
flora.caution: Extremely dry and flammable; keep away from unintended open flames. Do not ingest.

processing: **Tinder:** Cut hard outer shell off. The soft, suede-like brown layer inside is the 'Amadou'. Slice thin. Fluff it up. One spark will catch it and it smolders for hours (coal extender).

flora.name: Birch Polypore
flora.identification: Shelf fungus on birch trees. Smooth, grey/brown top, white underside.
flora.uses: Anti-parasitic, styptic, immune support. 'Nature's Band-Aid'.
flora.caution: Has a very bitter taste. Ensure proper identification to avoid harvesting toxic look-alike tree fungi.

processing: **Tea:** Slice and boil to release immune-boosting beta-glucans.
**Band-Aid:** Peel a strip of the mushroom's white underside (pore layer) to use as a naturally sterile, adhesive bandage.

flora.name: Calendula (Pot Marigold)
flora.identification: Bright orange/yellow daisy-like flowers. Sticky green stems.
flora.uses: Skin healing, anti-inflammatory. Petals are edible.
flora.caution: May cause allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to the Asteraceae family (daisies, ragweed).

processing: **Salve:** Infuse dried petals in oil for 4-6 weeks to create a powerful skin-healing balm for burns and cuts.

flora.name: Comfrey (Knitbone)
flora.identification: Large, hairy leaves. Bell-shaped purple or cream flowers.
flora.uses: Speeds healing of bones and sprains (Allantoin). Leaf mulch for gardens.
flora.caution: Do not use on deep open wounds (heals surface too fast). Do not ingest large amounts (liver concern).

processing: **Poultice:** Mash fresh leaves and apply to closed fractures, sprains, or bruises to rapidly reduce swelling.

flora.name: Echinacea (Coneflower)
flora.identification: Purple petals, spiky orange/brown center cone.
flora.uses: Immune stimulant for cold/flu.
flora.caution: Avoid continuous use for more than 8 weeks. Do not use if you have autoimmune conditions or are sensitive to ragweed.

processing: **Tincture:** Infuse roots or flower heads in high-proof alcohol for 6 weeks. Take at first sign of illness.

flora.name: Oregon Grape
flora.identification: Holly-like leaves, yellow flowers, blue-purple tart berries.
flora.uses: Bright yellow inner bark/root is high in Berberine (antibiotic). Berries for jelly.
flora.caution: Berries are very tart; roots are extremely bitter.

details.habitat: Rocky soil, mountain forests, urban landscaping.
processing: **Antibiotic:** Harvest the yellow root. Dry and decoct for digestive infections or skin fungus.

flora.name: Peppermint
flora.identification: Square stem, opposite leaves. Strong minty scent.
flora.uses: Digestion, headaches, cooling effect.
flora.caution: Can spread aggressively in gardens.

processing: **Tea:** Fresh or dried leaves. Excellent for calming an upset stomach or cooling down on a hot day.

flora.name: Usnea (Old Man's Beard)
flora.identification: Lichen hanging from trees. Grey-green. Pull gently; it has a stretchy white inner core.
flora.uses: Powerful natural antibiotic and antifungal. Edible (but bitter).
flora.caution: Pulls heavy metals from air - do not harvest near roads.

processing: **Identification:** If it doesn't have the 'rubber band' white core when stretched, it isn't Usnea.
**Medicine:** Contains Usnic acid. Best extracted in alcohol (tincture) or simmered in water for a long time.

flora.name: Wild Strawberry
flora.identification: Low-growing, three serrated leaflets, small white flower with 5 petals, tiny intensely flavored red berries.
flora.uses: Berries eaten raw or preserved. Leaves used for tea (Vitamin C).
flora.caution: None. Ensure ID to avoid 'Mock Strawberry' (edible but tasteless).

details.harvesting: Harvest when deep red. They are tiny but pack 10x the flavor of store-bought berries.
processing: **Tea:** Air-dry young leaves. Steep 1 tsp in hot water. High in Vitamin C and good for digestion.
**Preservation:** Due to small size, they are best as 'top-shelf' jam additions or eaten fresh.

flora.name: Mulberry
flora.identification: Tree with varied leaf shapes (unlobed to multi-lobed). Fruit looks like a long blackberry.
flora.uses: Berries eaten fresh, dried, or in pies. Wood for smoking meat.
flora.caution: Unripe berries and milky sap can cause mild stomach upset or hallucinations.

details.harvesting: Shake tree over a sheet to collect ripe berries safely.
processing: **Drying:** Sun-dry for a shelf-stable raisin-like snack.
**Pies/Jams:** Use like blackberries but expect a milder, sweeter flavor.

flora.name: Crabapple
flora.identification: Small, deciduous tree. Five-petaled white/pink spring blossoms. Fruit is a small apple (under 2" diameter), often tart or bitter.
flora.uses: High-pectin source for jellies. Cider, sauces, pickled fruit.
flora.caution: Seeds contain amygdalin (cyanide-precursor). Do not ingest seeds in large quantities.

details.habitat: Abandoned orchards, forest edges, suburban landscapes.
details.harvesting: Harvest in late fall after first frost for best sugar content. Smaller fruits are generally higher in pectin.
processing: **Jelly:** Boil whole fruits with water until soft. Strain. High pectin means no store-bought pectin is usually needed to set.
**Sauce:** Use like standard apples but add significantly more sweetener (honey/maple syrup).
**Pickled:** Small crabapples can be pickled whole in a spicy vinegar brine.

flora.name: Black Walnut
flora.identification: Large deciduous tree. Bark is dark and furrowed into diamond shapes. Compound leaves with 15-23 leaflets. Nuts are encased in thick, round green husks.
flora.uses: Nut meats (rich, oily, earthy). Green husks for dye and medicinal anti-parasitic. Wood is premium lumber.
flora.caution: Hulls contain Juglone—stains skin and clothing black. Stains are permanent on many surfaces.

details.habitat: Rich, moist bottomlands, floodplains, and open sunny fields.
details.harvesting: Gather fallen nuts in late September/October. Test for ripeness by pressing with your thumb—it should dent.
processing: **1. Hulling:** Remove green/black husks immediately. Modern survival trick: Drive over them with a vehicle to break the hulls, or use a manual corn sheller. WEAR GLOVES.
**2. Washing:** Place in a bucket of water. 'Floaters' are likely bad; 'sinkers' are good. Rinse until clean.
**3. Curing:** Dry in a cool, ventilated place (hanging mesh bags are ideal) for 2-3 weeks. The nut is ready when the meat snaps rather than bends.
**4. Cracking:** Requires a heavy-duty nutcracker or hammer. Extract meats with a pick.
**5. Storage:** Stored in shells in a cool place, they last up to a year. Once shelled, freeze immediately due to high oil content.

flora.name: Maple Trees (Sugar/Red/Silver)
flora.identification: Opposite branching (v-shapes). Palmately lobed leaves (hand-shaped). 'Helicopter' winged seeds (samaras). Sugar maples have rounded 'U' shapes between lobes; Red maples have sharp 'V' shapes.
flora.uses: Sap for syrup and sugar. Inner bark (cambium) is emergency fuel/fodder.
flora.caution: None. Ensure you tap only healthy, mature trees (at least 10-12 inches diameter).

details.harvesting: Sap flows when nights are below freezing (32°F) and days are above freezing (40°F+).
processing: **1. Tapping:** Drill a 5/16" or 7/16" hole about 2 inches deep, angled slightly upward. Insert a 'spile' (metal or wood tube).
**2. Collecting:** Hang buckets or jugs. A single tree can produce 10-20 gallons of sap in a season.
**3. Boiling:** Sap is roughly 98% water. Boil down in a wide, flat pan. Ratio is approx. 40:1 (40 gallons of sap makes 1 gallon of syrup).
**4. Finishing:** Once the liquid reaches 7°F above the boiling point of water (approx. 219°F), it is syrup. Filter through felt while hot to remove 'niter' (sand-like calcium deposits).
**5. Tree Care:** Remove spiles at the end of the season. The tree will naturally heal the hole in one growing season.

flora.name: Wild Mustard
flora.identification: Four-petaled yellow flowers in an 'X' or cross shape (Brassicaceae family). Long, thin seed pods (siliques) that stick out from the stem. Leaves are often lobed and spicy/peppery.
flora.uses: Young leaves in salads/sautés. Seeds for homemade mustard. Flowers as garnish.
flora.caution: Avoid large quantities if you have thyroid issues (contains goitrogens). Ensure identification to avoid similar-looking toxic plants.

details.habitat: Disturbed soil, roadsides, agricultural edges, and sunny fields.
details.harvesting: Harvest leaves in early spring while tender. Collect mature brown seed pods in mid-to-late summer.
processing: **Greens:** Steam or sauté to mellow the peppery bite. Excellent high-vitamin side dish.
**Mustard Paste:** Grind dry seeds into powder. Mix with cold water and a splash of vinegar/salt. Let sit for a few hours to develop heat.
**Oil:** In survival, seeds can be crushed and pressed for a spicy edible oil.

flora.name: Wild Peas / Beach Peas
flora.identification: Vining plant with tendrils. Compound leaves with pairs of leaflets. Flowers are pea-shaped, often purple, pink, or white. Seed pods look like small garden peas.
flora.uses: Cooked peas (after leaching/boiling).
flora.caution: CRITICAL: Many species of Lathyrus (like Sweet Pea) are TOXIC and contain neurotoxins that cause Lathyrism (paralysis). *Lathyrus japonicus* is generally considered edible but MUST BE BOILED in multiple changes of water. Never eat large quantities. DO NOT eat if unsure of exact species.

details.harvesting: Harvest pods while green and plump. Avoid dry, brown pods unless saving for seed (not for eating).
processing: **Boiling:** Shell the peas. Boil in plenty of water for 10 minutes, discard water, and repeat. This helps remove potential toxins. Eat in small quantities only.
**Identification Check:** Ensure the plant has THE SAME features as a pea (tendrils, pea flowers). Look out for toxic lupines which have palmately compound leaves (like fingers).

flora.name: Horseweed / Marestail
flora.identification: Tall, erect stem (up to 6ft). Hairy leaf margins. Many narrow, alternating leaves. Tiny, inconspicuous white/yellow flower heads at the top.
flora.uses: Seasoning (peppery). Dried leaves for tea (astringent).
flora.caution: Some people experience skin irritation from the hairy leaves.

details.habitat: Fields, disturbed soil, gardens, and urban waste areas.
details.harvesting: Harvest young leaves and tender tops before the plant flowers (top 6-12 inches).
processing: **Seasoning:** Dry the young leaves and crumble them into soups or stews as a substitute for black pepper. It has a distinct, spicy resinous flavor.
**Tea:** Steep dried leaves for an astringent tea used traditionally to treat digestive upset.

flora.name: Wild Violet
flora.identification: Heart-shaped leaves with slightly serrated edges. Flowers have 5 petals, typically purple or white with a 'bearded' throat. Low-growing basal rosette.
flora.uses: Leaves (extremely high in Vit C and A). Flowers for jellies, syrups, and as edible garnish.
flora.caution: Yellow violets can be mildly laxative; focus on purple/white varieties. Do not consume African Violets (houseplants), which are not true violets and are toxic.

details.habitat: Lawns, shady forest edges, and damp meadows.
details.harvesting: Pick leaves and flowers in early spring. Leaves remain edible through summer but become tougher.
processing: **Salad:** Use fresh leaves as a base—they are mild and highly nutritious.
**Violet Syrup:** Steep purple flowers in hot water for 24 hours. Strain. Add sugar/lemon juice. The lemon juice will cause the blue liquid to turn a vibrant pink/purple.
**Poultice:** Macerate leaves for a soothing skin treatment for minor abrasions.

flora.name: Amaranth (Pigweed)
flora.identification: Tall, erect stems (up to 5-8ft). Terminal flower spikes that are often red, green, or purple. Alternate, oval to spear-shaped leaves. Stems often have a reddish tint at the base.
flora.uses: Young leaves as spinach-like greens. Mature seeds as a high-protein, gluten-free grain.
flora.caution: Nitrate accumulator; avoid harvesting from heavily fertilized fields or industrial areas.

details.habitat: Disturbed soil, agricultural fields, and waste areas.
details.harvesting: Harvest leaves in spring/early summer. Collect seeds in late fall by shaking the mature flower heads into a bucket.
processing: **Greens:** Steam or sauté young leaves. They are richer in protein, iron, and calcium than traditional spinach.
**Grain:** Winnow the seeds to remove the chaff. Boil 1 part seed to 2 parts water for 15-20 minutes. It has a slightly nutty, earthy flavor.
**Popped Amaranth:** Small seeds can be toasted in a hot, dry skillet until they pop like miniature popcorn.

flora.name: Clovers (Red / White)
flora.identification: Trifoliate leaves (three leaflets), often with a white 'V' marking. Round, dense flower heads made of many tiny tubular flowers. Red clover has purple-pink heads; White clover has white/pinkish heads.
flora.uses: Flower heads for nutritive tea or flour additive. Young leaves in salads or as potherbs.
flora.caution: Raw leaves are difficult for humans to digest in large quantities (bloating). Red clover contains isoflavones; use in moderation during pregnancy.

details.harvesting: Gather fresh flower heads and young leaves in spring and early summer.
processing: **Tea:** Steep fresh or dried red clover blossoms for a sweet, nutritious tea traditionally used for blood purification and respiratory support.
**Flour:** Dry the flower heads and grind them into a powder to extend standard flour in breadmaking.
**Cooking:** Sauté young leaves with other wild greens to improve digestibility.

flora.name: Acorns
flora.identification: Nut produced by Oak trees. Oval or round nut encased in a woody 'cap'. White oaks have rounded leaf lobes and less bitter acorns; Red oaks have pointed leaf lobes and higher tannin (more bitter) acorns.
flora.uses: Primary survival carbohydrate. Flour for bread, pancakes, and thickening stews.
flora.caution: CRITICAL: MUST LEACH. Raw acorns contain high levels of tannins (tannic acid), which are bitter and puckering, and can cause kidney damage in large quantities.

details.habitat: Forests, parklands, and suburban oak groves.
details.harvesting: Gather fallen nuts in September/October. Discard any with small holes (weevils) or caps still firmly attached (usually immature).
processing: **1. Shelling:** Crack the outer shell and remove the nut meat.
**2. Grinding:** Grind the nut meats into a coarse meal using a mortar and pestle or food processor.

**3. Cold Leaching (Best for Flour):** Place meal in a jar of cold water. Shake, let settle, and pour off the dark water. Repeat daily until the meal no longer tastes bitter (usually 3-7 days). This preserves the starch for better binding.

**4. Hot Leaching (Fastest):** Boil meal in multiple changes of water. Discard water when it turns dark and add fresh boiling water. Repeat until bitterness is gone. Note: This 'cooks' the starch, making it better for mush/porridge but worse for bread.
**5. Drying/Storage:** Once leached, spread meal thin to dry. Once fully dry, grind into a fine flour and store in a cool, dark place.

flora.name: Coltsfoot
flora.identification: Yellow dandelion-like flowers appear ON SCALY STEMS before the leaves emerge. Leaves are heart-shaped or 'colt's foot' shaped, surfacing later with a white, felt-like underside.
flora.uses: Traditional salt substitute (leaf ash). Respiratory tea (limited use).
flora.caution: Contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids; do not consume in large quantities or over long periods. Do not use during pregnancy.

details.habitat: Clay banks, road cuts, ditches, and wet disturbed soil.
details.harvesting: Collect leaves in late spring/early summer once they are full-size.
processing: **Survival Salt (The Ash Method):** Dry the large leaves thoroughly until brittle. Burn the leaves on a clean surface (like a flat rock or metal tray). The remaining white/gray ash is rich in potassium and was traditionally used as a savory salt substitute in many cultures.
**Cough Remedy:** Steep a small amount of dried leaf for tea to treat dry coughs. Filter through cloth to remove the fuzzy leaf hairs.

flora.name: Wild Sunflowers
flora.identification: Tall, rough/hairy stems. Bright yellow flower heads with a dark or yellow center. Heart-shaped, serrated leaves that feel like sandpaper. Flowers always track the sun across the sky.
flora.uses: Seeds (highly nutritious, high fat). Flower buds (eaten like artichokes). Oil extraction.
flora.caution: None. Very high calorie-to-effort ratio in survival.

details.habitat: Sunny prairies, roadsides, and open fields.
details.harvesting: Harvest seed heads in fall once the back of the head turns yellow/brown and the seeds are plump.
processing: **Eating:** Roast seeds in their shells. High in Vitamin E and essential fatty acids.
**Oil Extraction:** In a survival context, crush the de-shelled seeds and boil them in water. The oil will float to the top and can be skimmed off for cooking or as a high-calorie supplement.
**Flower Buds:** Steam young, unopened flower buds for 10-15 minutes. Serve with butter/salt—tastes remarkably like artichoke.

flora.name: Chamomile
flora.identification: Small daisy-like flowers with white petals and yellow centers. Feathery leaves. Smells like apples when crushed.
flora.uses: Sleep aid, digestive calmative, skin soothing.
flora.caution: May cause allergic reaction in people sensitive to the Asteraceae family (ragweed, daisies).

processing: **Tea:** Steep fresh or dried flower heads (not leaves) for 5-10 minutes. Famous for promoting sleep and easing anxiety.
**Digestive:** Drink after meals to reduce gas and bloating.
**Skin:** Use cooled tea as a wash for inflamed skin or as a compress for tired eyes.

flora.name: Self-Heal (Heal-All)
flora.identification: Square stem (mint family). Spiky purple flower head. Oval leaves.
flora.uses: Broad-spectrum medicinal. Wound healing, sore throats, antiviral.
flora.caution: None.

processing: **Wound Wash:** Strong decoction used to wash cuts. Very effective at stopping bleeding and preventing infection.
**Tea:** Used for internal inflammations and as a general tonic.
**Edible:** Young leaves can be eaten raw in salads.

fauna.name: White-Tailed Deer
fauna.notes: Primary large game. Crepuscular (active dawn/dusk).

details.behavior: Crepuscular (active dawn/dusk). Follows food sources (acorns, corn, clover). Alerts: tail flag, snort.
details.shot_placement: Broadside: Aim just behind the shoulder, 1/3 up from the brisket (heart/lung). Quartering away: Aim for off-side shoulder.
processing: **1. Field Dressing (Gutting):** Do this immediately to cool meat. Cut from pelvic bone to brisket (careful not to punture stomach). Spill guts.
**2. Skinning:** Hang by rear legs. Cut around hocks and peel hide down like a sock. Use knife sparingly.
**3. Quartering:** Remove front shoulders (floating bone), rear hams (ball joint), backstraps (run knife along spine), and tenderloins (inside cavity).
**4. Butchering:** Remove silver skin. Separate muscle groups. Cut against grain for steaks, grind scraps for burger.
**5. Tanning Hide:** Scrape all flesh/fat. Salt heavily for 2 days. Rehydrate, pickle in acid solution, break fibers while drying.
details.utilization: Meat (Food), Hide (Leather/Buckskin), Antlers (Tools/Buttons), Sinew (Cordage/Thread), Bones (Broth/Tools).

fauna.name: Cottontail Rabbit
fauna.notes: Plentiful but low fat ('Rabbit Starvation' risk if eaten exclusively).

details.behavior: Freezes when threatened. Zig-zag run. Lives in brush piles. Active early morning/late evening.
processing: **1. 'Jacket' Skinning:** No knife needed. Pinch hide on back, pull apart until it tears. Pull skin opposite ways (like taking off a jacket). Pull off legs.
**2. Gutting:** Pinch belly, slice up to ribs, down to pelvis. Swing rabbit downward firmly to eject guts (centrifugal force).
**3. Disease Check:** ALWAYS inspect the liver. If it has white spots/cysts, discard the entire animal (Tularemia). Do not feed to dogs.
**4. Cooking:** Low fat meat. Best stewed or braised with added fat (bacon/oil) to prevent dryness.
details.utilization: Meat, Fur (very warm, but thin skin - best for lining gloves/hats).

fauna.name: Black Bear
fauna.notes: Generally shy but dangerous around cubs or food. Hang food bags 10ft high.

details.behavior: Omnivore. Excellent smell. Climb trees well.
processing: **1. Safety:** Wear gloves. Bears carry Trichinosis (parasite).
**2. Rendering Fat:** Bear grease is liquid gold. Skin carefully to keep fat on carcass or hide. Cube fat, render on low heat. shelf stable, waterproof, cooking oil.
**3. Meat:** Dark, sweet meat. MUST be cooked to 165°F (well done) to kill parasites. Never eat rare.
**4. Hide:** Very heavy/greasy. Requires extensive fleshing/degreasing before tanning.
details.utilization: Fat (Oil/Grease/Fuel), Meat, Fur (Rugs/Blankets).

fauna.name: Coyote
fauna.notes: Pack hunter. Scavenger. Keep pets close.

details.behavior: Opportunistic. Lures dogs away to pack. Vocalizations (yips/howls) indicate numbers.
processing: **Fur:** Prime in winter. 'Case skin' (tube) for market.
**Meat:** Generally not eaten (scavenger), but edible in survival. Boil thoroughly.
**Bones:** Can be used for tools/needles.

fauna.name: Eastern Gray Squirrel
fauna.notes: Abundant, calorie-dense small game. Easy to hunt/trap.

details.behavior: Diurnal. Mast eater (nuts). Noisy.
processing: **Skinning (Tail Method):** Cut through tail bone and skin around rear legs. Step on tail. Pull rear legs up. Hide strips off like a shirt. Quick and clean.
**Cooking:** Tough meat. Slow cook/stew is best. 'Squirrel Pot Pie'.
details.utilization: Meat, Tail (Fly fishing lure/Decoration).

fauna.name: Wild Turkey
fauna.notes: Large bird. Wary eyesight. Roosts in trees at night.

details.behavior: Flocks. Ground feeder. Extremely sharp vision (wear camo).
processing: **Plucking:** Dipping in hot water (140°F) makes feathers release easier. Or just skin it for faster processing.
**Meat:** Breast meat is substantial. Legs/Thighs are tough/tendon-heavy (slow cook for soup).
details.utilization: Meat, Feathers (Fletching arrows), Bones (Calls).

fauna.name: Beaver
fauna.notes: Aquatic engineer. High fat content (critical in winter).

details.behavior: Nocturnal. Dams/Lodges. Slaps tail on water to warn.
processing: **Castor Glands:** Save the scent glands near tail (bait for other traps).
**Tail:** Roast over fire. Skin bubbles off. Inside is fatty gristle (energy boost).
**Fur:** Prime winter warmth.
details.utilization: Meat (Rich/Dark), Fur, Castor, Tail.

fauna.name: Mallard Duck
fauna.notes: Common waterfowl. Male has green head.

details.behavior: Ponds/Rivers. Dips head to feed (dabbler).
processing: **Plucking:** Keep the down feathers! Excellent insulation for pillows/jackets.
**Fat:** Render the fat. Great cooking oil.
details.utilization: Meat, Down (Insulation), Fat.

fauna.name: Moose
fauna.notes: Largest member of the deer family. Highly dangerous during rut. Found near water/marshes.

details.behavior: Solitary and aquatic-feeding. Aggressive during rut (Sept/Oct). Signs of aggression: ears pinned back, hair on neck standing up, lip licking. 'Bluff charges' are common but can turn into committed charges if the animal feels cornered.
processing: **1. Field Quartering:** Due to sheer size (800lb-1500lb), moose must often be processed where they fall. Use the 'gutless method' to remove quarters without opening the abdominal cavity.
**2. Swing Skinning:** If a tripod or heavy branch is available, skin while hanging to prevent meat from touching the dirt. Moose hide is exceptionally thick and requires a very sharp blade.
**3. Cooling:** Meat of this thickness spoils rapidly (bone sour). Quarters must be hung in breathable game bags immediately. Remove the 'brisket' and 'hump' as they contain high-value fat/muscle.
details.utilization: Meat (substantial calorie source), Nose Leather (traditional delicacy, rich in collagen), Hide (extremely durable heavy-duty leather), Sinew (leg tendons provide the strongest natural cordage for bowstrings/tools).

fauna.name: Elk (Wapiti)
fauna.notes: Large herd animal. Known for the male's distinct 'bugle' during rut.

details.behavior: Highly social herd hierarchy. They move to higher elevations in summer and valleys in winter. Use thermal cover (thick timber) during the day. Bugling is a primary identification marker in autumn.
processing: **1. Antler Removal:** Cut at the skull plate. Antlers are useful for tool handles and pressure flakers.
**2. Hindquarter Breakdown:** Large muscle groups like the 'Top Round' and 'Sirloin' should be separated at the seams to maintain quality.
**3. Backstrap Extraction:** Run the knife along the spine from the neck to the pelvis to remove the primary tenderloin.
details.utilization: Meat (Prized high-protein game), Antlers (Tools/Handles/Calcium source for dogs), Hide (Lighter than moose, superior for clothing).

fauna.name: Grizzly / Brown Bear
fauna.notes: Distinguishable by the shoulder hump and dish-shaped face. Highly territorial.

details.behavior: Omnivore with significant seasonal caloric needs. Distinguishing from black bears: Grizzlies have a prominent shoulder hump, a concave/dish-shaped face profile, and much longer, straighter claws. Defensive behavior: If attacked, 'Play Dead' (lie on your stomach, protect your neck) to indicate you are not a threat.
processing: **1. Rendering Fat:** Grizzly fat is high-density energy. Slice into 1-inch cubes and render on low heat to produce shelf-stable 'bear grease'.
**2. Meat Safety:** Like all bears, grizzlies carry Trichinella. Meat MUST be cooked to an internal temperature of 165°F. Never eat rare bear meat.
details.utilization: Fat (Grease for waterproofing/cooking), Fur (Heavy winter insulation), Claws/Teeth (Historical/Decorative utility).

fauna.name: Gray Wolf
fauna.notes: Pack hunter. Larger than coyotes with blockier features.

details.behavior: Social pack hunters with complex hierarchy. Highly intelligent. Distinguish from coyotes by the blockier snout, smaller rounded ears (proportionally), and deep, resonant howls vs coyote 'yips'.
defense: **Pack Deterrents:** If followed, do not run. Face the pack, maintain height, and use loud, aggressive vocalizations. Keep fires bright at night; wolves are naturally wary of the 'red flower'.
details.utilization: Fur (Extremely warm, ice doesn't stick to wolf fur—ideal for parka ruffs), Teeth (Survival needles/tools).

fauna.name: Mountain Lion (Cougar)
fauna.notes: Ghost of the woods. Ambush predator. Rarely seen but always watching.

details.behavior: Solitary ambush predator. Hunts by stalking and pouncing. Caches kills by covering them with leaf litter/snow—finding a 'drag' or buried carcass is a sign of an active cat in the area.
safety: **Contact Rules:** NEVER turn your back or run (triggers chase reflex). Maintain eye contact, stand ground, and make yourself look larger. Fighting back with everything available is the only option if attacked.
details.utilization: Identification of 'cat-scratches' (territorial markings) on trees helps map their range. Meat is edible (tastes like pork) but generally avoided due to their role as apex predators.

fauna.name: American Bison
fauna.notes: The massive icon of the plains. Formidable and unpredictable.

details.behavior: Grazer. Moves in large family units. Unpredictable temper; a bison's tail standing straight up is a sign of an imminent charge. They can run at 35mph.
utilization: **1. Meat:** Exceptional nutrient density, high in minerals.
**2. Hump:** High-value fat storage used for making Pemmican (long-term survival ration).
**3. Hide:** Historically used for tepee covers, winter robes, and industrial belting.
**4. Bone/Bladder:** Bladders were used as water containers; bones for dozens of tools (scrapers, needles, hoes).

fauna.name: Feral Hog (Wild Boar)
fauna.notes: Highly intelligent, destructive, and aggressive. Extreme population growth.

details.danger: Boars possess 3-inch razorsharp tusks and can weigh 400lb+. Sows with piglets are exceptionally defensive. Carries pseudorabies, brucellosis, and numerous parasites.
details.behavior: Nocturnal or crepuscular. Generally travel in 'sounders' (groups of sows and young). Boars are often solitary.
processing: **1. Scalding vs Skinning:** Traditional harvest involves scalding in 145°F water to scrape hair, preserving the calorie-rich skin. Otherwise, skinning requires careful navigation of the 'shield' (thick cartilage on a boar's shoulders).
**2. Field Dressing:** Must be done immediately to cool the meat. Wear gloves to prevent zoonotic disease transfer.
**3. Cooking:** Meat MUST reach an internal temperature of 160°F-165°F to ensure parasite destruction.
details.utilization: Meat (Wild pork—lean and flavorful), Fat (Lard for baking/preservation), Hide (Tough leather).

fauna.name: Raccoon
fauna.notes: Dexterous and clever scavengers. Primary rabies vector.

processing: **1. Gland Removal:** Raccoons have axillary (armpit) and inguinal (groin) glands that must be removed immediately after skinning. If left, they impart a strong, unpleasant musk to the meat.
**2. Fat Removal:** In autumn, raccoons carry heavy fat layers. Most should be trimmed as the fat flavor can be overwhelming.
details.utilization: Meat (dark, rich meat), Grease (rendered fat for industrial/leather usage), Fur (classic winter hats/trim).

fauna.name: Bobcat
fauna.notes: Secretive feline. Short tail and tufted ears.

details.behavior: Elusive and solitary. Hunts rabbits and rodents. Identification: Direct-register tracks (rear foot lands in the print of the front foot) create a single line of prints through snow/mud.
details.utilization: Pelts (Prized for softness and spots), Identification of range helps map small game availability.

fauna.name: Red Fox
fauna.notes: Highly adaptable. Iconic white-tipped tail.

details.behavior: Cunning and clever. Mousing behavior involves high-pouncing to break through crusty snow. Vocalizations include 'barks' similar to a small dog and blood-curdling 'screams' during mating season.
details.utilization: Fur (prime winter pelt is extremely warm/soft), Skulls (tools/ornamental usage).

fauna.name: American Badger
fauna.notes: Low-slung, powerful digger. Notoriously aggressive.

details.behavior: Primary burrower. They create massive network dens. Known to hunt mutualistically with coyotes (coyote chases prey above ground, badger blocks burrows).
details.defense: Will hiss, growl, and charge if cornered. Thick hide and loose skin make it difficult for predators to secure a fatal grip.

fauna.name: Wolverine
fauna.notes: Smallest 'big' predator. Fierce and tireless traveler.

details.behavior: Solitary and territorial. Can travel 30 miles a day in harsh terrain. Known as the 'Skunk Bear' due to the powerful musk glands used to mark territory and food caches.
details.survival: Total avoidance of active territories is advised. Wolverines have been known to drive bears and cougars off kills.

fauna.name: North American Porcupine
fauna.notes: Slow-moving rodent with specialized defense quills. Major survival resource.

details.harvest: Known as the 'Survivalist's Best Friend' because it is slow and can be harvested with a simple blunt object (stick/club) in an emergency. They do not 'throw' quills, but the quills detach upon contact.
processing: **1. Quill Collection:** Carefully remove patches of quills. They can be cleaned and used as heavy-duty sewing needles, awls, or for ornamental quillwork.
**2. Skinning:** Skin from the belly up to avoid the quill-heavy back. Porcupine meat is edible but can be 'piney' depending on their diet.
details.utilization: Meat (emergency calories), Quills (Tools/Art).

fauna.name: Striped Skunk
fauna.notes: Docile but equipped with a powerful chemical deterrent.

details.behavior: Crepuscular. Defensive behavior includes stomping front feet and raising the tail. Spotted skunks (related) may even perform 'handstands' before spraying.
details.processing: If harvested for meat, the scent glands (located near the anus) MUST be removed with surgical precision. If punctured, the meat and processor will be contaminated for days.
details.utilization: Meat is edible and similar to rabbit if glands are avoided. Scent signs help identify predator density in an area.

fauna.name: Virginia Opossum
fauna.notes: North America's only marsupial. 'Plays dead' as a defense mechanism.

details.utility: Exceptional tick control (one opossum can eat 5,000 ticks a season). They have a very high resistance to snake venom and rarely carry rabies due to their low body temperature.
details.behavior: Nocturnal. When threatened, they may enter an involuntary catatonic state ('playing possum') that can last for hours.

fauna.name: Pronghorn
fauna.notes: Fasteness land animal in North America. Not a true antelope.

details.behavior: Extremely keen eyesight (equivalent to 8x binoculars). High-speed running (55mph+). Curiosity: Historically lured closer by waving a flag or 'flagging' to trigger their investigative nature.
details.utilization: Meat (distinctive sage-like flavor), Hide (very thin and breathable leather).

fauna.name: Bighorn Sheep
fauna.notes: Rugged mountain dwellers. Rams have massive curved horns.

details.habitat: High-altitude rocky terrain. Their presence indicates stable water sources and alpine grazing. Navigation around sheep requires understanding their 'escape terrain' (cliffs where they outclimb predators).
details.utilization: Meat (high-quality wild mutton), Horns (historically used for composite bows and spoons).

details.behavior: Defensive only near hive. Dies after stinging.
processing: **Stings:** Scrape stinger out with credit card (don't pinch it, that injects more venom). Apply Plantain poultice.
**Honey:** Antiseptic, energy, never spoils. Apply to wounds to prevent infection.
**Wax:** Melt comb to make candles, waterproofing for leather/canvas, or salve base.

insects.name: Monarch Butterfly
insects.identification: Large orange wings with black veins and white spots.

details.behavior: Migratory. Toxic to birds due to milkweed diet.
details.details: Indicator species for environmental health. Plant milkweed to support them.

insects.name: Deer Tick
insects.identification: Size of poppy seed. Reddish-brown back.
insects.notes: Carrier of Lyme Disease. Check creases of body.

details.habitat: Tall grass, leaf litter. Questing (holding legs up waiting for host).
processing: **Removal:** Do NOT burn, smother (vaseline/oil), or twist. This makes them vomit into your blood.
**Technique:** Use pointy tweezers. Grasp head as close to skin as possible. Pull straight up. Cleaning bite area.
**Lyme Signs:** Watch for 'Bullseye' rash (Erythema migrans) expanding from bite. Fever, aches. Seek meds immediately.

insects.name: Mosquito
insects.identification: Small midge-like fly. High pitched whine.
insects.notes: Vector for disease. Breed in standing water.

processing: **Prevention:** Eliminate standing water. Wear light colors.
**Natural Repellents:** Smoke (smudge fires), Yarrow, Beautyberry, Cedar oil.
**Itch Relief:** Jewelweed juice, Plantain poultice, Mud, cool water.

details.behavior: Ambush predator. Harmless to humans.
details.details: Garden guardian. Eats pests. Egg cases (Ootheca) overwinter on twigs - do not destroy.

insects.name: Black Ant
insects.notes: Emergency snack. Tangy citrus taste (Formic Acid).

details.behavior: Social. Colonies.
details.details: Edible raw or roasted. Don't eat red fire ants (sting).

insects.name: Termite
insects.identification: White/cream soft body. Lives in rotting wood.

details.behavior: Colonies in dead wood.
details.details: Roast them. Avoid eating the wood grit. High fat/protein.

insects.name: Cricket / Grasshopper
insects.identification: Leaping insects. Crickets are usually black/brown; Grasshoppers vary in color.
insects.notes: High protein, low fat. Nutty flavor when roasted.

details.caution: Always cook thoroughly to kill parasites. Remove large legs and wings before eating as they are scratchy and non-nutritious.
processing: **Catching:** Best caught in early morning when they are sluggish from the cold.
**Preparation:** Freeze for 20 mins to kill humanely. Dry roast in a pan until brittle. Toss with salt or chili powder.

insects.name: Cicada
insects.identification: Large, loud insects with transparent wings. Emerges from ground.
insects.notes: Tastes like 'shrimp of the land'. High in protein.

details.caution: Avoid if you have a shellfish allergy (related proteins).
processing: **Harvesting:** Best eaten just after they emerge from their shells (teneral stage) while they are still soft and white.
**Preparation:** Remove wings and legs. Boil for 4-5 minutes then sauté or fry.

aquatic.name: Largemouth Bass
aquatic.habitat: Lakes, ponds, and slow rivers with heavy cover (weeds, logs, docks).
aquatic.behavior: Aggressive ambush predator. Most active at dawn and dusk. Moves to deep water in midday heat.
aquatic.best_bait: Live minnows, worms, crawfish. Lures: Jigs, spinnerbaits, plastic worms.

details.processing: Bleed and gut immediately. Filleting is the standard method. Mild flavor.
details.utilization: Meat (High protein), Skin (Fragile but can be tanned for small items).

aquatic.name: Smallmouth Bass
aquatic.habitat: Clearer, cooler water than largemouth. Rocky bottoms and moving current.
aquatic.behavior: Strong fighter. Feeds on crawfish and small minnows. Often school around rock piles.
aquatic.best_bait: Crayfish (live or lures), small jigs, inline spinners.

details.processing: Same as largemouth. Firmer meat, highly prized.
details.utilization: Meat.

aquatic.name: Northern Pike
aquatic.habitat: Cool, weedy shallows in summer; deeper drop-offs in winter.
aquatic.behavior: Fierce predator with razor teeth. Ambush hunter in weed beds.
aquatic.best_bait: Large spoons, spinners, suckers, or large minnows. Requires wire leader.

details.processing: Slime coat is heavy; wipe down with vinegar or salt. Bony (Y-bones) require specialized filleting technique.
details.utilization: Meat, Skin (Can be tanned into very strong fish leather).

aquatic.name: Walleye
aquatic.habitat: Deep pools, gravel bars, and wind-blown points in large lakes/rivers.
aquatic.behavior: Nocturnal sight hunter. Eyes reflect light. Move to shallows at night to feed.
aquatic.best_bait: Leeches, nightcrawlers, minnows. Jigs with bright tails.

details.processing: The 'Gold Standard' of freshwater eating. Firm, flaky white fillets. Check cheeks for succulent small medallions.
details.utilization: Meat.

aquatic.name: Channel Catfish
aquatic.habitat: Rivers, lakes, and ponds. Prefers current and structure.
aquatic.behavior: Keen sense of smell and taste. Feed most actively at night and in murky water.
aquatic.best_bait: Stink bait, chicken liver, cut fish, nightcrawlers.

details.processing: CAUTION: Poisonous spines on dorsal/pectoral fins. Skinning is required; use pliers. Remove the 'mud vein' (lateral line).
details.utilization: Meat, Skin (Durable leather), Oil (Rendered from fat).

aquatic.name: Rainbow Trout
aquatic.habitat: Cold, oxygenated rivers and lakes. Current breaks.
aquatic.behavior: Surface feeders in hatch season; move to deep pools in summer. Jump when hooked.
aquatic.best_bait: Insects (flies), salmon eggs, worms, small spinners.

details.processing: Delicate meat. Can be cooked whole or filleted. Best fresh; spoilage is rapid.
details.utilization: Meat (High Omega-3s).

aquatic.name: Chinook (King) Salmon
aquatic.habitat: Oceans/Great Lakes; spawns in cold freshwater rivers.
aquatic.behavior: Massive spawning runs. Stop feeding in rivers but strike out of aggression.

details.processing: Oil content is extremely high. Bleed immediately for best flavor. Ideal for cold smoking.
details.utilization: Meat (Calorie dense), Roe (Nutrient bomb), Skin.

aquatic.name: Yellow Perch
aquatic.habitat: Clear water with weed beds. Often in large schools.
aquatic.behavior: Daytime feeders. Travel in schools; if you catch one, there are dozens more.

details.processing: Small but easy to clean. Scaled and fried whole or filleted.
details.utilization: Meat (The most reliable mass-catch species).

aquatic.name: Bluegill (Sunfish)
aquatic.habitat: Everywhere. Shallow weeds, docks, fallen trees.
aquatic.behavior: Opportunistic. Will bite almost anything small. Excellent 'first catch' for beginners.

details.processing: Scaled and gutted. Cooked whole over a fire.
details.utilization: Meat (Survival staple).

aquatic.name: Common Carp
aquatic.habitat: Murky lakes and slow rivers with soft bottoms.
aquatic.behavior: Wary and powerful. Sucks food off the bottom. Spawns in shallows in spring with much splashing.

details.processing: Heavy scales. Dark meat with many small bones. Soaking in saltwater/milk removes 'muddy' taste.
details.utilization: Meat (Massive calorie yield), Industrial scales.

aquatic.name: Lake Sturgeon
aquatic.habitat: Large river systems and Great Lakes. Deep holes.
aquatic.behavior: Ancient, armor-plated dinosaur. Scent-based feeder. Lives over 100 years.
aquatic.best_bait: Smelly bait: cut fish, crawfish, gizzard shad.

details.processing: No scales, but bony plates (scutes). Firm, meat-like texture. No bones (cartilaginous skeleton).
details.utilization: Meat (Premium), Isinglass (from swim bladder), Leather.

aquatic.name: Crayfish (Crawdad)
aquatic.habitat: Rocky stream beds, under stones, lake edges.
aquatic.behavior: Nocturnal. Scavengers. Burrow into mud in droughts.
aquatic.best_bait: Anything meaty in a trap (fish guts, chicken neck).

details.processing: Purge in clean water for 30 mins. Boil for 5-7 mins until red. Peel tails.
details.utilization: Meat, Excellent bait for larger predatory fish.

tracking.name: Deer Track
tracking.description: Heart-shaped. Two toes. 2-3 inches long. Sharp edges indicate freshness.
tracking.gait: Diagonal Walker (Rear foot lands on front track)

tracking.name: Rabbit Track
tracking.description: The 'Y' shape. Two long rear feet land *in front* of two small front feet.

tracking.name: Canine (Coyote/Dog)
tracking.description: Oval shape. 4 toes. Claws visible (X shape between toes).

tracking.name: Feline (Bobcat/Cougar)
tracking.description: Round shape. 4 toes. NO claws visible (retractable). Asymmetric leading toe. Cougars are significantly larger (3-4") than bobcats (2").
tracking.gait: Direct Walker (Rear foot lands in front print)

tracking.name: Raccoon
tracking.description: Looks like a small human hand (5 long fingers).

tracking.name: Scat: Herbivore
tracking.description: Pellets (Deer/Rabbit) indicate browsing. Piles (Moose/Bison) indicate grazing. Fibrous plant matter visible. Freshness indicated by moisture and shine.

tracking.name: Scat: Predator
tracking.description: Tubular, often segmented (Canine) or tapered (Feline). Contains fur, bones, or seeds. White color (calcification) indicates old kill/bone consumption.

tracking.name: Turkey Track
tracking.description: Large 'Arrow' shape. 3 distinct toes pointing forward. 4 inches long.

tracking.name: Black Bear Track
tracking.description: Hind foot looks like a barefoot human (5 toes, large heel pad). Front foot smaller.

tracking.name: Moose Track
tracking.description: Large, cloven, heart-shaped (6-7 inches). Much larger than deer.

tracking.name: Gray Wolf Track
tracking.description: 4.5-5 inches long. Claw marks converge toward center. Linear trail (unlike meandering dog).

tracking.name: Bison Track
tracking.description: Rounded cloven lobes (4-5 inches). Larger and circular compared to cattle.

tracking.name: Squirrel Track
tracking.description: Blocky bounder pattern. Front paws (4 clones) land behind/inside rear paws (5 toes).

tracking.name: Porcupine Track
tracking.description: Pigeon-toed (toes point in). Pebble-like texture on pads. Often shows tail drag.
